title: Extracellular Y RNA fragments in gastrointestinal cancer and a proposed role for YBX1 in macrophage responses.
abstract: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) can alter macrophage responses, but the contribution of individual RNA cargoes remains difficult to establish. Y RNA-derived fragments are candidate mediators whose mechanisms after EV exposure have not been conclusively defined across physiological settings. This review examines reported EV-associated macrophage effects in gastrointestinal (GI) cancer, Y RNA studies from other diseases, and a possible role for RNA modifications and RNA-binding proteins. Separate experimental systems link YBX1 protein methylation to fragment sorting, damage-associated Y3 RNA methylation to YBX1 binding and PARP1 activity, and extracellular hY4 to monocyte responses through TLR7. These observations do not establish a continuous pathway in GI cancer. We propose that a sequence-defined Y RNA fragment could reach recipient macrophages, bind YBX1 in an m5C-sensitive manner, and alter a measurable molecular process before changing macrophage function. Whether this occurs, whether RNA methylation precedes or follows transfer, and whether the response supports tumor growth remain unresolved. A cardiac study using a synthetic Y RNA fragment reported reduced inflammatory-cell recruitment, illustrating that RNA responses can differ with disease and treatment context. The review distinguishes vesicle uptake from functional RNA delivery and considers endosomal sensing, other EV cargoes, and donor-cell effects as alternative explanations. Testing this hypothesis will require demonstrating functional delivery of a defined Y RNA fragment and YBX1-dependent macrophage effects in the same GI cancer model.

title: The CCCH-type zinc-finger PfMD3 promotes translation for malaria parasite transmission.
abstract: Sexual maturation and fertility of the malaria-causing parasite, Plasmodium spp., are critical to transmission between hosts. This developmental process involves an intricate gene expression regulatory network that drives gametocyte commitment, development, and the production of male and female gametes. Here, we characterize the role of the CCCH-type zinc-finger protein Plasmodium falciparum Male Development 3 (PfMD3) in the formation of gametes. Genetic disruption of PfMD3 reveals a male fertility defect that decreases infectivity to mosquitoes. Molecular characterization of PfMD3 reveals its binding to mRNA transcripts is associated with male gamete development through a specific RNA sequence. Gametocyte proteins encoded by these PfMD3-bound transcripts decrease significantly in PfMD3 knockout parasites, suggesting that PfMD3 impacts translation. In addition to RNA-binding, PfMD3 also interacts with proteins involved in mRNA processing and nuclear export that influence translational regulation. This study establishes PfMD3 as an RNA-binding protein that impacts lineage-specific translation and male gamete fertility.

title: Holistic integration of protein interaction datasets establishes a framework for exploring the organization and composition of Caenorhabditis elegans germ granules.
abstract: Spatiotemporal organization of biological molecules is a key driver of cellular processes, including many post-transcriptional epigenetic processes. The germline-specific germ granules are biomolecular condensates that act as hubs for mRNA and small RNA processing and are core regulators of germline gene expression programming. Germ granules have been studied extensively in Caenorhabditis elegans, and recent developments have led to many subdivisions of the germ granule into specialized compartments. Rapid advancements in microscopy and protein-protein interaction (PPI) screening techniques have produced a large amount of data towards characterizing the localization of proteins to specific granules. However, common methods used to probe PPIs are limited in their ability to robustly detect valid interactions, especially the multivalent and sometimes transient ones observed in granule environments. Here we perform a meta-analysis of granule protein interaction screens. While these experiments generally enrich for proteins matching the profile of granule-associated proteins, we find that when considering screens individually, reproducibility is surprisingly low, highlighting not only the variability inherent in these methods but also the dynamic nature of the PPI networks present in granules. We developed an algorithm to provide a measure of each protein's association with specific granules across various experiments (a "granule association metric" or GAM). By further clustering and investigation of the GAM matrix, we demonstrate the power of this holistic approach to provide deeper insights into germ granule organization, highlight novel candidates, and act as a resource to inform future investigations into granules and their constituent proteins.

title: First mitogenome-based phylogenetic analysis and divergence time estimation of deep-sea elasipodid sea cucumbers (Holothuroidea: Elasipodida).
abstract: Elasipodida is a major deep-sea holothuroid order, and distributed across depths ranging from 350 m to 7,000 m. Its high species diversity and extensive bathymetric range make it a key model system for investigating the evolutionary processes and adaptive radiation of deep-sea fauna. The mitogenome is characterized by several advantages, such as maternal inheritance, small size, fast evolutionary rates and low recombination. Moreover, it serves as an effective molecular marker for resolving phylogenetic relationships and reconstructing divergence histories in holothuroids. However, the scarcity of complete mitochondrial genome sequences from elasipodid species has substantially hindered resolution of the phylogenetic relationships among constituent families and reconstruction of their divergence history. This study reports, for the first time, the complete mitochondrial genomes of four deep-sea elasipodid species: Laetmogone violacea, Enypniastes eximia, Psychropotes longicauda, and Benthodytes sp. The four mitogenomes exhibit substantial length variation (16,500 to 18,757 bp) while retaining the canonical metazoan gene complement of 37 genes. All four species exhibited negative AT-skew values. Amino acid composition analysis revealed a pronounced preference for leucine. Each species possesses a full set of 22 transfer RNA (tRNA) genes, including duplicated copies of trnL and trnS. Phylogenetic analyses robustly support two major clades within the order Elasipodida: the Psychropotidae-Pelagothuriidae clade and the Elpidiidae-Laetmogonidae clade. The 13 protein-coding genes exhibit identical gene order across the 18 examined holothuroid species, except for the inverse transposition of nad6 in E. eximia; in addition, tRNA gene rearrangements were detected. Divergence time estimation indicates that the stem lineage of Elasipodida likely originated by the Middle Devonian (387 Ma), with the crown radiation of the order beginning in the Middle Permian (262.77 Ma). Collectively, this study establishes a foundational mitogenomic dataset and provide a robust scientific foundation for future studies on the temporal divergence and evolutionary history of elasipodid sea cucumbers.

title: BCLAF1 links RNA splicing to ATF4-dependent metabolic adaptation in acute myeloid leukemia.
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by genetic alterations and non-mutational mechanisms that disrupt normal hematopoiesis and support leukemic cell survival. While the mutational landscape of AML is well characterized, the non-genetic processes sustaining leukemic maintenance remain less understood. Using human AML cells and murine models, we identify BCL2-associated transcription factor 1 (BCLAF1) as a key regulator of leukemic progression through control of mRNA processing. BCLAF1 physically associates with core spliceosome components and regulates alternative splicing programs in leukemic cells. Mechanistically, BCLAF1 is required for productive splicing of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) mRNA, thereby sustaining ATF4 protein levels and downstream metabolic gene expression programs. Loss of BCLAF1 reduces ATF4 levels, leading to impaired de novo amino acid biosynthesis and increased sensitivity to venetoclax. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism linking RNA splicing control to metabolic adaptation in AML, identifying BCLAF1 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

title: HMGB1 expression in CT26 murine cancer cells modulates the tumor microenvironment and limits local anti-tumor immunity.
abstract: High mobility group box protein 1 (HMGB1) is a ubiquitous protein that has multiple functions in the nucleus and cytosol. Following release into the extracellular space, HMGB1 acts as a mediator of inflammation. HMGB1 is overexpressed in many cancers and has both oncogenic and antitumoral effects. Here we investigated the role of HMGB1 expression by cancer cells in the antitumor immune response. Subcutaneous tumors were induced in mice by injection of wild-type or HMGB1-low engineered syngeneic cancer cells. Tumor growth and immune infiltration were assessed, and gene expression was analysed in whole tumors and isolated tumor cells by RNA sequencing analysis. Downregulation of cancer cell-intrinsic HMGB1 prevented tumor growth and reprogrammed the tumor microenvironment into a more inflamed phenotype. Tumor growth was not impacted in immunodeficient mice or in mice deficient in CD8+ T cells, demonstrating that the impact of HMGB1 downregulation on tumor progression was immune-dependent and mediated by CD8+ T cells. Transcriptional profiling showed that HMGB1low tumors were enriched in immune pathways such as antigen presentation, T-cell receptor and cytokine signalling. Immune activation was robust and detectable in both tumor tissue and secondary lymphoid organs of mice bearing HMGB1low tumors, but this did not facilitate immune infiltration of wild-type tumors that had been co-injected in the contralateral flank. We propose that tumor cell-intrinsic HMGB1 plays a critical role in modulating the local tumor microenvironment and in limiting anticancer immune responses. Thus, targeting cancer cell-intrinsic HMGB1 may represent a novel approach to improve the outcome of cancer immunotherapy.

title: A Novel Workflow to Assess Serum Stability of Antibody-siRNA Conjugates.
abstract: Antibody-siRNA conjugates (ARCs) are emerging as a promising approach for targeted delivery of small interfering RNA (siRNA) to specific cells outside the liver, harnessing the advantages of antibody-based delivery to overcome limitations inherent to siRNA molecules, including rapid degradation, limited tissue penetration, and poor specificity. To address the critical need for robust stability assessment of ARCs in biological matrices, we developed a novel in vitro serum stability assay featuring immunoaffinity purification that purified a tool molecule, ARC1, under neutral conditions from biological matrices to preserve the molecular integrity and prevent artificial degradation. The purified ARC1 was analyzed in three complementary liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) methods: native mass spectrometry, protein mass spectrometry, and oligonucleotide mass spectrometry. This assay enabled assessment of each individual ARC component, including the parental antibody, linker, sense strand, and antisense strand. The results demonstrated that the linker remained stable in serum for 4 days, while hydrolysis of the conjugated siRNA occurred in both sense and antisense strands. Various biotransformation products were identified by mapping the results from three LC-HRMS methods to visualize the degradation pathway of ARC1. This work represents the first in vitro serum stability analysis workflow of ARCs that can capture biotransformation of each ARC component using immunoaffinity purification. This method offers a valuable tool to proactively identify potential liabilities in ARC designs and inform ARC candidate selection, siRNA engineering, and strategic planning for bioanalytical, toxicity, and immunogenicity assessment during drug discovery and early development.

title: Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan Attenuates Neuronal Injury in LPS-Treated HT22 Cells and PCPA-Induced Insomnia-Model Rats.
abstract: Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan (TWBXD) is traditionally used for sleep disorders, but its neuroprotective mechanisms remain unclear. This study evaluated a cinnabar-free modified TWBXD preparation in cellular and animal models, focusing on phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) expression, autophagy-related markers, inflammation, and apoptosis. An aqueous TWBXD extract was profiled by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Candidate compounds annotated by LC-MS and checked against PubChem records were used for target prediction, followed by intersection with insomnia-related genes, protein-protein interaction analysis, and functional enrichment. TWBXD-containing serum was evaluated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-treated HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Rapamycin and 3-methyladenine were used to probe autophagy-related processes. In p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA)-treated rats, pentobarbital-induced sleep responses, locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, spatial learning and memory, and hippocampal CA1 pathology were assessed. Twenty high-confidence candidate compounds yielded 553 predicted human targets, of which 144 overlapped with insomnia-related genes. Network analysis identified 10 candidate hub genes, including AKT1, MTOR, BCL2, TNF, and IL6, and highlighted PI3K-Akt, autophagy, apoptosis, and inflammatory pathways. In LPS-treated cells, rapamycin shifted several autophagy-related and inflammatory markers toward control levels. TWBXD-containing serum increased Beclin 1 expression and the microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3-II to light chain 3-I (LC3-II/LC3-I) ratio, decreased p62, interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), Bax, and caspase 3, and increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) and Bcl-2. PI3K and AKT protein and messenger RNA (mRNA) levels also shifted toward control levels. Several TWBXD-associated molecular changes were attenuated by 3-methyladenine. In PCPA-treated rats, TWBXD improved pentobarbital-induced sleep responses, anxiety-like behavior, and spatial learning and memory and alleviated hippocampal CA1 neuronal injury. These findings support the neuroprotective effects of cinnabar-free modified TWBXD in the models examined. Behavioral and histological improvements were accompanied by changes in PI3K/AKT expression and autophagy-, inflammation-, and apoptosis-related markers.

title: Immune Regulation by Regnase-1 and Related Endoribonucleases.
abstract: Regnase-1 (ZC3H12A) is a stem-loop (SL)-recognizing endoribonuclease that couples immune stimulation to selective mRNA decay. Although originally characterized as a negative regulator of inflammatory cytokine expression, recent studies have expanded this view by placing Regnase-1 within a broader network of SL-recognizing RNA decay factors, including Roquin proteins and Regnase-3, and by revealing context-dependent functions in immune and nonimmune cells. Through regulation of transcripts encoding cytokines, costimulatory molecules, and transcriptional regulators, Regnase-1 restrains innate and adaptive immune activation, but biological output varies according to cell type, tissue environment, disease stage, and mode of perturbation. In T cells, including engineered T cells used in adoptive cell therapy, Regnase-1 inhibition can enhance antitumor activity in preclinical models, whereas in epithelial tissues Regnase-1 can limit inflammatory circuits that affect host defense, tissue injury, and inflammation-associated tumorigenesis. Structure-targeting antisense oligonucleotides and genome-editing approaches have further raised the possibility of therapeutically modulating Regnase-dependent RNA decay. In this Review, we discuss molecular mechanisms of Regnase-1-mediated mRNA decay, context-dependent functions across tissues and diseases, and the opportunities and limitations of targeting this pathway therapeutically.

title: Recombinant Fusion of Polyglutamic Acid Enhances Cell-Penetrating Peptide-Mediated CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery.
abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

title: The Impact of Different Isolation Methods on Extracellular Vesicle Yield and Composition in human Breast Milk: A Pilot Study.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) play a key role in intercellular communication and are present in diverse physiological fluids, including breast milk (BM). Evidence has suggested that BM-derived EVs (BMEVs) impact the health and well-being of infants. To gain insights into the biochemical composition and functionality of BMEVs, effective isolation with minimal contamination is essential. Various methods have been utilised for BMEV isolation, each with inherent advantages and limitations. This pilot study compares three isolation methods-ultracentrifugation (UC), size exclusion chromatography (SEC), and multimodal chromatography with a charged core bead Capto Core column (CC)-to determine the most efficient approach for enriching BMEVs from small BM sample volumes. BMEVs were isolated from samples collected from three donors using UC, SEC, and CC. BMEV yields and cargo were evaluated using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), BCA protein quantification, western blotting, proteomics, and small RNA sequencing. NTA showed similar particle concentrations and size distributions across all three isolation methods, and TEM validated the presence of EVs. Particle-to-protein ratios differed significantly across isolation methods, with SEC showing a significantly higher ratio than UC. Western blot and proteomics analyses showed greater enrichment of EV-associated proteins in SEC and CC compared to UC, while CC showed the lowest abundance of BMEV contaminants (alpha-S1-casein, lactoferrin and α-lactalbumin). UC captured a distinct miRNA profile including higher enrichment of hsa-miR-16-5p compared to other methods. Based on our findings, the CC isolation method may serve as a viable approach for isolating an EV-enriched fraction from BM. CC was more effective at reducing co-isolated contaminants compared to UC or SEC, while maintaining enrichment of EV-associated proteins. Additionally, CC-based isolation is cost-effective, user friendly, and highly scalable, thus making it a potential practical and efficient solution for both routine research and large-scale clinical applications.

title: Antiviral effects of traditional herbal medicine Otsu-Ji-To against human coronavirus OC43, SARS-CoV-2, and its variants: in vitro and in vivo studies.
abstract: Otsu-Ji-To (OJT), also known as Eul-ja-tang in Korean, is a traditional herbal formula used to treat hemorrhoids. We investigated its antiviral effects against HCoV-OC43, SARS-CoV-2, and its variants. Antiviral activity was determined using qRT-PCR, Western blot analysis, immunofluorescent staining assay, plaque reduction assay, or CPE reduction assay. UHPLC-QTOF MS/MS and UHPLC-MRM analyses were used to identify and quantify the OJT's chemical markers. To determine the mode of action, SARS-CoV-2 Mpro and PLpro activity assay kits and a cell-based RdRp activity assay system were used. SARS-CoV-2- or Omicron variant-infected K18-hACE2 transgenic mice and hamsters in vivo experiments were conducted. We found that OJT inhibited HCoV-OC43 (IC50 = 674.9 μg/mL), SARS-CoV-2 (IC50 = 236.5 μg/mL), and its variants by reducing viral RNA and protein expression levels as well as attenuating cytopathic effects in vitro. We identified and quantified seven compounds from OJT's herbal components. Baicalein, liquiritigenin, emodin, and rhein exhibited anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity by lowering viral protein expression levels. Furthermore, OJT inhibited the SARS-CoV-2 viral Mpro and PLpro in enzymatic activity assays as well as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in a cell-based assay. In vivo, oral administration of OJT to wild-type SARS-CoV-2- or Omicron variant-infected K18-hACE2 transgenic mice and hamsters increased survival rates, reduced viral RNA and protein levels, or improved lung histology, suggesting OJT's therapeutic potential for treating COVID-19. These results suggest that OJT could be a promising therapeutic agent for treating coronavirus infections.

title: Nano-enabled approaches in virology: emerging strategies for rapid detection, antiviral therapy, and biomimetic innovation.
abstract: Global health continues to be impacted by viral diseases, and this poses a need for timely diagnosis, potent antiviral treatment, and flexible prevention. To tackle these problems, nanotechnology has become an incredibly flexible tool for viral detection, therapeutic delivery, vaccination and biomimetic material design. Recent developments in the field of nano-enabled virology will be reviewed and will focus on the use of nanomaterials in the development of biosensors and diagnostic platforms to make virus detection more sensitive, specific, faster and more portable. It also explores the antiviral activity of metallic, polymeric, lipid-based, carbon-based and 2D nanomaterials, including MXenes, their ability to directly inactivate viruses and targeted delivery of antiviral agents and nucleic acids, etc. Special focus is placed on lipid nanoparticles as carriers for RNA therapeutics and mRNA vaccines, and novel vaccine strategies based on peptides, proteins, virus-like particles, and DNA. Virus-templated and virus-inspired nanomaterials are also included in the review and are considered as biomimetic platforms for the controlled fabrication of functional nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on MXenes, which are currently being explored for the detection and application against viruses, due to their tunable surface chemistry and potential future applications, and challenges associated with stability, toxicity, and translation are highlighted. Finally, ongoing translational issues such as safety, toxicity, production, regulatory issues and the development of experimental platforms to clinical application are addressed.

title: Metabolic Memory in Oral Inflammation.
abstract: The global rise in metabolic diseases has increased the severity and therapeutic complexity of oral inflammatory disorders. Persistent inflammation driven by metabolic memory presents a central pathological mechanism. Even after metabolic parameters are normalized, abnormal gene expression can persist, leading to prolonged disease progression and recurrent episodes. In the oral cavity, metabolic memory is most clearly evident in periodontitis and impaired wound healing, where sustained immune dysregulation and tissue destruction remain after hyperglycemia or hyperlipidemia has been corrected. Epigenetic reprogramming presents a key molecular mechanism of metabolic memory, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and expression of noncoding RNAs. The epigenetic alterations collectively reprogram immune cell function, driving the dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunity while influencing the fate of oral stromal cells and epithelial cells. Prolonged inflammation contributes to an altered host-microbiota interaction, reinforcing disease persistence and treatment resistance. Metabolic disorders induce coordinated epigenetic changes that can be grouped into permissive and repressive events affecting gene transcription. Permissive events include increased histone acetylation, enrichment of activating histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K4me3), and DNA demethylation at inflammatory gene loci. These modifications promote an open chromatin structure to enhance transcription factor access. Repressive events include increased DNA methylation and enrichment of repressive histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K9me3). DNA methylation typically occurs in promoter regions of genes, and repressive histone changes lead to the formation of compact chromatin, both of which reduce transcriptional activity. Noncoding RNAs generally decrease target messenger RNA stability or inhibit translation further, reinforcing a repressive effect. The combined effect of these modifications is a shift in protein expression that reinforces chronic inflammatory signaling in abnormal metabolic conditions. This review comprehensively summarizes the epigenetic mechanisms by which metabolic memory sustains oral inflammation at molecular, cellular, and tissue levels, as well as potential preventive and therapeutic interventions.

title: Melatonin ameliorates renal fibrosis by disrupting the DANCR/QK-mediated stabilization of MALAT1 and inhibiting Galectin-3-dependent macrophage polarization.
abstract: Renal fibrosis drives kidney dysfunction in chronic kidney disease via inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibroblast activation. Deciphering its mechanisms is vital for antifibrotic therapy. A mouse model of renal fibrosis was established via unilateral ureteral obstruction, with melatonin treatment administered. Exosomes from human kidney 2 (HK-2) cells were characterized and co-cultured with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-induced M0 macrophages. Macrophage polarization was analyzed via flow cytometry. Gene‑interaction studies were performed, including ribonucleic acid (RNA) immunoprecipitation, pull-down, and luciferase reporter assays. Melatonin treatment decreased metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (MALAT1) expression in TGF‑β1‑treated HK‑2 cells, alleviated collagen deposition, and improved renal function in vivo. Mechanistically, melatonin disrupted the interaction between differentiation antagonizing non-protein coding RNA (DANCR) and the RNA‑binding protein quaking (QK), thereby destabilizing MALAT1 to downregulate Galectin‑3, which in turn inhibited both M1/M2 macrophage polarization. HK‑2‑derived exosomal MALAT1 was transferred to macrophages, promoting polarization, and administration of MALAT1‑overexpressing exosomes abolished melatonin's protective effects in vivo. Melatonin destabilizes MALAT1 by suppressing DANCR-associated QK, thereby reducing Galectin-3 to restrain macrophage polarization and mitigate renal fibrosis. Several limitations exist: a single acute animal model, lack of macrophage-specific MALAT1 knockout mice, and absence of clinical validation.

title: Small Nucleolar RNAs, Big Impact: Biogenesis, Mechanisms, and Roles in Health and Disease.
abstract: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are a diverse class of regulatory molecules classified by their size, localization, and function. Among them, small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are 60-300-nucleotide small non-coding RNAs that are primarily encoded within intronic regions of protein-coding or non-coding host genes. They are broadly categorized into three types: C/D box snoRNAs (SNORDs), H/ACA box snoRNAs (SNORAs), and Cajal body-specific RNAs (scaRNAs). SNORDs and SNORAs primarily mediate RNA modifications through 2'-O-methylation (Nm) and pseudouridylation (Ψ), respectively, whereas scaRNAs specialize in modifying small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) within the Cajal body, which is crucial for splicing processes. Recent discoveries have broadened the functional landscape of snoRNAs beyond their canonical roles, uncovering non-canonical functions in protein secretion and the identification of snoRNA/scaRNA reads within glycoRNA-associated small RNA populations, suggesting novel mechanisms of cellular communication and pathophysiology. This review offers an integrative discussion of snoRNAs, focusing on their biogenesis, functions, developmental roles, and implications in various diseases, while providing detailed insights into these RNAs.

title: Detection and whole-genome characterisation of Regana virus in the bicoloured shrew (Crocidura leucodon) from Graubünden, Switzerland.
abstract: Orthonairoviruses are of medical and veterinary importance, but the genetic diversity and geographic distribution of shrew-associated orthonairoviruses remain unclear. Shrews are increasingly recognised as hosts for diverse orthonairoviruses, including Regana virus (REGV), which has been reported in the bicoloured white-toothed shrew (Crocidura leucodon) in Germany and the Czech Republic. We examined archived shrew specimens collected in Graubünden Canton, Switzerland, between 2005 and 2006 using nested reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, pairwise sequence comparison, and protein feature annotation. Nairoviral RNA was detected in three C. leucodon from Luzein and Malans, whereas four Sorex araneus and one Neomys anomalus tested negative. Complete or near-complete REGV genome sequences were recovered from the three positive animals. Swiss REGV variants clustered with REGV from Germany and the Czech Republic across the S, M, and L segments. RdRp amino acid identities were 98.8-98.9% among Swiss variants and 92.1-95.6% between REGV Np12 and German or Czech variants. Comparative protein analyses identified conserved viral ovarian tumour protease catalytic residues, similar glycoprotein precursor organisations, and nairovirus-like nucleoprotein motifs. These findings document REGV in C. leucodon in Switzerland and expand the known geographical and genetic ranges of REGV in European shrew populations.

title: Rational design of lipid nanoparticles for brain delivery of RNA therapeutics.
abstract: Effective delivery of RNA therapeutics to the brain remains challenging due to the multiple barriers of the central nervous system (CNS). To probe molecular scaffolds that could help overcome these barriers, we analysed the pharmaceutical profiles of over 100 CNS-active drugs and identified hydroxyzine (HX) as a promising scaffold for designing ionizable lipids with improved brain-targeting properties. Specifically, HX1 liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) achieved robust mRNA delivery to the brain through multiple trafficking pathways across CNS barriers. HX1 LNPs also enabled efficient gene editing in mouse brains via co-delivery of CRISPR mRNA and guide RNA and effectively delivered luciferase mRNA to the brain of a non-human primate. Moreover, HX1 LNPs carrying Il10 mRNA mitigated radiation-induced brain injury in mice, highlighting their potential for preventive treatment in the presence of intact CNS barriers. These findings establish HX1 LNPs as a promising translational platform for delivering therapeutic mRNAs and genome-editing components to the brain.

title: Gegen Qinlian Decoction Alleviates DSS-induced Colitis Through Modulation of Intestinal Stem Cell Homeostasis and M1 Macrophage Polarization.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) imposes a significant burden on human health and socioeconomic systems. Gegen Qinlian Decoction (GQD) is an effective formula clinically used for the treatment of IBD. However, the underlying mechanisms of GQD in treating colitis remain incompletely elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic effects of GQD in DSS-induced colitis mice, and explore the underlying mechanisms, thereby providing novel perspectives and strategies for colitis treatment. A mouse colitis model was induced by administering 2.5% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) in drinking water. The therapeutic efficacy of GQD was assessed by monitoring body weight, disease activity index (DAI), colon length, histopathological damage, inflammatory cytokines, and intestinal mechanical and mucus barrier function. RNA sequencing was performed to reveal the underlying mechanisms. The effects of GQD on macrophage polarization and intestinal stem cells (ISCs) restoration were subsequently examined. GQD treatment significantly alleviated DSS-induced colitis and tissue damage, accompanied by restoration of tight junction protein expression and improvement of mucus barrier function. RNA sequencing suggested that the effects of GQD in colitis mice were closely associated with ISCs and macrophage functions. Experimental validation demonstrated that GQD treatment was associated with increased expression of ISC-associated markers, including AXIN2, and improved goblet cell-associated mucus barrier parameters. Meanwhile, GQD treatment attenuated M1 macrophage polarization, accompanied by decreased inflammatory cytokine levels and alleviation of intestinal inflammation. These effects were also accompanied by reduced SNX10 expression and alterations in Wnt/β-catenin and NLRP3/caspase-1 signaling pathways. GQD ameliorates intestinal mucosal barrier function and promotes mucosal healing in DSS-induced colitis mice. These effects are associated with the upregulation of ISC-related markers expression and the inhibition of M1 macrophage polarization.

title: m6A-modified hsa_circ_0010996 regulates ferroptosis in anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury cells by binding to EIF4A3.
abstract: To investigate the expression and functional significance of N6-methyladenosine (m6A)-modified hsa_circ_0010996 in patients with anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury (ADLI) and cellular models, and to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which it regulates ferroptosis in ADLI cells through interaction with eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4A3 (EIF4A3). The expression levels of hsa_circ_0010996 in the serum of the study population and in HL-7702 cell models were quantified using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP)-qPCR was employed to assess the m6A modification levels of hsa_circ_0010996. The interaction between hsa_circ_0010996 and EIF4A3 was validated via RNA-binding protein immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays. The extent of ferroptosis was evaluated by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA), ferrous iron (Fe2+), and glutathione (GSH) levels. Furthermore, the expression of ferroptosis-related proteins, including glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), was analysed by Western blot. Hsa_circ_0010996 was significantly upregulated in the serum of ADLI patients and in ADLI cell models. Overexpression of hsa_circ_0010996 in HL-7702 cells accelerated ADLI progression and promoted ferroptosis. Mechanistically, fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO)-mediated m6A demethylation inhibited the degradation of hsa_circ_0010996. Hsa_circ_0010996 was found to bind to EIF4A3, with both molecules co-localising within the cytoplasm. Importantly, silencing of EIF4A3 alleviated hsa_circ_0010996-induced ferroptosis in ADLI cells. This study highlights the critical role of hsa_circ_0010996 in the pathogenesis of ADLI through the modulation of ferroptosis. Targeting the FTO/hsa_circ_0010996/EIF4A3 regulatory axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the prevention and treatment of ADLI.

title: Regulation of endogenous dsRNA: strategies for self-tolerance.
abstract: Cells must continuously distinguish cellular-derived RNA from pathogenic RNA to mount effective antiviral responses while avoiding harmful autoinflammation. Cytoplasmic RNA-sensing receptors, including RIG-I-like receptors, PKR, OAS-RNase L and ZBP1, detect RNA primarily through molecular features such as structure (double- versus single-stranded), modification state and subcellular localization rather than sequence. While these are characteristics of viral nucleic acids, mammalian genomes generate abundant self-derived double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), including from transposable elements, antisense transcription and RNA processing intermediates, which exist in the cytoplasm. This review describes our current understanding of how cells achieve self-tolerance through the active regulation of endogenous RNA. These mechanisms comprise epigenetic silencing of repetitive elements, RNA modifications (such as A-to-I editing and m6A), precise splicing, regulated nuclear export and decay, circRNA buffering, protein shielding and dedicated RNA degradation pathways. Insights from rare inherited monogenic interferonopathies and murine models illustrate how perturbations in these pathways lead to inappropriate activation of cytoplasmic RNA sensors and inflammatory disease when cellular dsRNA is mistakenly recognized as non-self. We highlight how dysregulated dsRNA homeostasis contributes to common autoimmune and neuroinflammatory disorders. Understanding how cells regulate endogenous dsRNA is crucial for defining disease mechanisms and developing new therapeutic strategies.

title: PEDV NSP5 promotes immune evasion by recruiting TRIM28 to degrade DDX3X.
abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) has emerged as the predominant swine enteric coronavirus, causing vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, and high mortality in piglets. Members of the DEAD-box family play critical roles in viral infection, yet their roles in PEDV infection remain undefined. Furthermore, it is unknown whether PEDV and its proteins regulate the expression of these DEAD-box proteins. In this study, reverse transcription quantitative PCR was used to examine the gene expression changes of 15 DEAD-box family members in the intestinal tissues of one-month-old PEDV-infected piglets. We found that the expression of DEAD-box helicase 3 X-Linked (DDX3X) was upregulated following PEDV infection, a result that was similarly observed in cellular experiments. Overexpression and knockdown of DDX3X significantly inhibited or promoted PEDV replication, respectively. Moreover, the use of specific DDX3X inhibitors demonstrated that DDX3X primarily restricts PEDV RNA accumulation. Our study also showed that DDX3X enhances RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling by promoting the phosphorylation of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), and Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence assays further demonstrated the association and colocalization of DDX3X with TBK1 and IRF3, potentially contributing to its antiviral function. We constructed all PEDV proteins and identified that NSP5 reduces DDX3X levels via ubiquitination. Additionally, we discovered that tripartite motif-containing protein 28 (TRIM28) interacts with DDX3X and mediates its K48-linked ubiquitination. Knockdown of TRIM28 significantly reduced NSP5-mediated DDX3X ubiquitination. In conclusion, this study clarified the molecular mechanism by which NSP5 antagonizes DDX3X-mediated antiviral immune responses via the ubiquitination pathway, providing new insights into PEDV-host interactions and potential targets for antiviral intervention.IMPORTANCERecurrent outbreaks of porcine epidemic diarrhea (PED) have led to substantial economic losses in the global swine industry. To proactively control PED, it is crucial to investigate the pathogenic mechanisms of PEDV, particularly by exploring the interactions between viral proteins and host factors. In this study, we identified a significant phenomenon: PEDV infection activates DDX3X, enhancing the antiviral activity of the RLR pathway, while PEDV NSP5 recruits TRIM28 to target DDX3X for degradation, thus suppressing immune responses. These findings shed light on the complex regulatory interplay between PEDV proteins and host factors, deepening our understanding of the role and mechanisms of PEDV NSP5 in immune suppression.

title: Long-Read Reference Transcriptomes for Five Species of Rosaceae Tribe Spiraeeae: A Resource for Investigating Sequence Divergence, Species-Associated Expression Variation, and Leaf-Developmental Candidate Genes.
abstract: Species in the Rosaceae tribe Spiraeeae occupy diverse habitats and vary strikingly in growth form and leaf morphology. Still, no reference transcriptomes have been published for the tribe, and its transcriptome-level variation is uncharacterized. We generated long-read (PacBio Iso-Seq) reference transcriptomes of five species spanning three genera: Petrophytum caespitosum (Nutt.) Rydb., Spiraea lucida Douglas ex Greene, Spiraea splendens Baumann ex K. Koch, Aruncus dioicus (Walter) Fernald var. dioicus, and Aruncus aethusifolius (H.Lév.) Nakai. We then quantified expression across 20 individuals using 3'-tag RNA sequencing (TagSeq) to characterize expression patterns, ortholog sequence divergence, and gene repertoire. Multivariate analyses (principal component analysis [PCA] and hierarchical clustering) resolved replicates into three groups corresponding to the sampled genera. Because the material combined field-collected and potted plants, we treat expression comparisons as descriptive and do not attribute them to genetic control of interspecific differences. Pairwise analyses revealed extensive transcriptional divergence between genera, including thousands of differentially expressed transcripts in comparisons such as A. aethusifolius vs. P. caespitosum. Functional enrichment highlighted variation in transport and catabolism, plastid organization, and biotic-stress responses, implicating both metabolic and organelle-associated processes. Transcription factor families, particularly bHLH and bZIP, varied most among differentially expressed transcripts. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) recovered modules correlated with species identity; because between-species variation dominates this dataset, we treat these as descriptive summaries of coexpression structure and do not regard them as independent evidence of species-specific regulatory programs. Because reads were quantified against a reference assembled from species-specific contigs, mapping rates were higher within species (70.5%-85.1%) than across species (25.1%-77.0%), and between-species expression comparisons are interpreted with this asymmetry in mind. Sequence-level analysis of orthologous transcript pairs indicated that protein-coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection. A small fraction (2.7%-5.0% of retained pairs) showed Ka/Ks > 1, but these were concentrated at low synonymous divergence, where ratio estimates are unstable; we therefore treat them as screening-level candidates for rapid divergence, enriched for stress-response, membrane-trafficking, and ion-transport annotations, and we make no claim of positive selection. These results provide a comparative transcriptomic framework for Spiraeeae and identify candidate transcripts and protein-coding differences for future studies of ecological and morphological variation in Rosaceae.

title: IGF2BP1 knockdown associates with alternative splicing changes of transcription factor genes in neuroblastoma cells.
abstract: IGF2BP1 is an oncofetal RNA-binding protein with oncogenic functions in neuroblastoma, but whether IGF2BP1 knockdown is associated with alternative splicing (AS) changes of transcription factor (TF) genes remains unclear. We re-analyzed RNA-seq data from IGF2BP1-knockdown BE(2)-C cells (three knockdown and three control samples). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and AS events (ASEs) were identified, followed by GO/KEGG enrichment. Differentially spliced genes were intersected with a human TF list. Isoform-specific qRT-PCR was performed in control and IGF2BP1-knockdown BE(2)-C cells to validate PSI changes. RIP-qPCR was used to test binding of IGF2BP1 to candidate TF mRNAs. ENCODE eCLIP-seq data from HepG2 and K562 cells were analyzed as indirect supportive evidence. We identified 807 DEGs and 3, 053 significant ASEs. Among genes with significant splicing changes, 64 were annotated as TFs; 20 splicing events corresponding to 18 genes passed stringent filtering. Independent qRT-PCR validated the PSI changes of LMO4 (A5SS), TCF7L2 (cassette exon), and EHMT2 (exon skipping), which correlated with RNA-seq predictions. RIP-qPCR confirmed that IGF2BP1 binds to LMO4, TCF7L2, and EHMT2 mRNAs in cells, but not to NCOR2. eCLIP-seq data from non-neuroblastoma cell lines provided indirect supporting evidence. IGF2BP1 knockdown is associated with widespread AS changes of TF genes in neuroblastoma cells, and IGF2BP1 binds to LMO4, TCF7L2, and EHMT2 mRNAs. These findings provide a correlative resource and hypotheses for future mechanistic studies; direct causality remains to be established.

title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions.
abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

title: Claustrum Transcriptome Alterations in Schizophrenia.
abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) is associated with transcriptome alterations in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), key regions in a distributed network that mediates cognitive functions impaired in the illness. The subcortical dorsal claustrum (dCLA) is structurally densely interconnected with the ACC and dlPFC and functionally coactivated with these regions during certain cognitive tasks. To identify SZ-associated transcriptome alterations in the dCLA. This case-control study used RNA sequencing data for dCLA homogenates from postmortem human brain of individuals with SZ and unaffected comparison (UC) individuals. Brain donations were obtained from the Allegheny County Office of the Medical Examiner, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Data analysis was performed from January 12, 2024, through May 22, 2026. Schizophrenia. Gene expression differences in the dCLA between individuals with SZ and UC individuals were the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included gene set enrichment in the dCLA and comparisons of gene expression differences across the dCLA, ACC, dlPFC, putamen, and caudate between individuals with SZ and UC individuals, including rank-rank hypergeometric overlap (RRHO) analyses. In the final dCLA samples from 96 individuals, including 47 individuals with SZ (10 [21.3%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.0 [13.3] years) and 49 UC individuals (10 [20.4%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.9 [14.2] years), there were 1717 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between individuals with SZ and UC individuals, with 1149 (66.9%) of the DEGs upregulated in SZ. Many upregulated DEGs were associated with immune response or transcription regulation, and many downregulated DEGs were associated with mitochondrial activity or oxidative phosphorylation. In comparisons between individuals with SZ and UC individuals with data from the dCLA, ACC, and dlPFC, the number of DEGs detected was 4 to 12 times greater in the dCLA (1242 DEGs) than in the ACC (289 DEGs) or dlPFC (102 DEGs). However, threshold-free RRHO analyses revealed a conserved pattern of SZ-associated gene expression alterations across all 3 regions. In comparison, concordance of gene expression alterations was lower with the putamen and caudate, subcortical regions with weaker connections to the dCLA. The results of this case-control study suggest that the dCLA is a prominent site of molecular alterations in SZ. These alterations might reflect the dCLA's extensive connectivity with affected cortical regions, distinctive intrinsic circuitry, and/or enrichment of vulnerable cell types.

title: Concurrent low-dose-rate gamma irradiation and inorganic arsenite: genotoxicity and transcriptional responses in liver and testis in CBA and C57BL/6 mice.
abstract: Humans in arsenic-endemic and radiologically exposed settings may be co-exposed to inorganic arsenic and ionizing radiation, yet the combined effects of chronic low-dose-rate irradiation and environmentally relevant arsenic are poorly defined. In a single factorial experiment, male CBA and C57BL/6N mice were exposed to sodium arsenite in drinking water (0, 0.3 or 3 mg/L) and chronic γ irradiation (2.5 mGy/h, total 3 Gy), alone and combined. We measured blood genotoxicity (comet and micronucleus assays), characterised 21 circulating miRNAs, global DNA methylation and sequenced liver and testis transcriptomes to identify significant pathways. Arsenite exposure was accompanied by an increase in FPG-sensitive DNA lesions in white blood cells alongside a slight reduction in single strand breaks. Micronucleus frequency in reticulocytes and erythrocytes was not affected by arsenite. Arsenite was identified as an oxidative rather than a chromosomal genotoxicant. Only one miRNA (miR-133a-5p) responded clearly to arsenite. Global DNA methylation was only affected by irradiation. The liver and testis transcriptomes shared common DNA-repair and oxidative-stress pathways, but the organs diverged in response. Irradiation was the dominant stressor while the effect of the concurrent arsenite exposure was additive, antagonistic or synergistic. Baseline strain differences were large but additive, with negligible strain × treatment interaction in the transcriptome, whereas strain × arsenite interactions were found for the FPG-comet signal and hepatic arsenic. Our study contributes new data, experimental design and analysis methods about the genotoxic and transcriptional landscape of multiple stressor exposure.

title: Iguratimod Modulates M1 Macrophage Polarization Via the NOTCH4-KLF4 Axis to Alleviate Antibody-Mediated Rejection.
abstract: Iguratimod (IGT) is a small-molecule anti-inflammatory agent that effectively attenuates the progression of antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR). However, the underlying mechanism of action of IGT remains poorly understood. Thus, this study aimed to investigate the mechanism through which IGT regulates macrophage polarization and ABMR. A mouse model of ABMR was established by performing kidney transplantation after skin graft-induced sensitization. Experimental interventions included neurogenic locus notch homolog protein 4 (NOTCH4) knockout mice and oral administration of IGT. RNA sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting (WB), flow cytometry, and immunofluorescence (IF) staining were performed to investigate M1 macrophage polarization and the Jagged1-NOTCH4 signaling pathway. This study found that IGT significantly reduced M1 macrophage infiltration into renal allografts in a mouse model of ABMR. Transcriptomic sequencing and subsequent biological experiments indicated that IGT may regulate macrophage polarization through the Jagged1-NOTCH4 pathway. M1 macrophage polarization may contribute to the initiation and progression of ABMR following kidney transplantation. IGT attenuates M1 macrophage polarization by inhibiting Jagged1-NOTCH4-Krüppel-like Factor 4 (KLF4) signaling.

title: Triterpenoid saponins from the aerial parts of Phytolacca americana and their anti-influenza A virus activity.
abstract: Phytolacca americana L. (Phytolaccaceae), a perennial species native to North America, is rich in oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins. In this study, ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-QTOF-MS) profiling of the aerial-part extract revealed characteristic fragment ions of phytolaccagenin- and phytolaccagenic acid-type saponins with diverse glycosylation. MS-guided annotation enabled targeted isolation and structural elucidation of two previously undescribed compounds, one oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin (1) and one neolignan (3). Additionally, compound 2, which had been reported only based on mass spectrometric data, was isolated, and its structure was fully elucidated for the first time, together with those of 10 known oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins (4-13). Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive one-dimensional and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic analyses combined with UPLC-QTOF-MS data. Although P. americana extracts have been reported to inhibit influenza A virus infection in previous studies, the bioactive constituents responsible for this antiviral activity have not been identified. The crude extract and isolated saponins were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. In H1N1-infected A549 cells, compound 11 (3-O-trisaccharide phytolaccagenic acid) reduced viral NS1 RNA levels at 6 and 24 hpi as determined by RT-qPCR. Antiviral activity was further confirmed by plaque reduction and immunoblot analyses, with a plaque-assay IC50 of 57.98 ± 0.26 µM.

title: Multi-omics dissection of interactive cross-stress tolerance to Penoxsulam and salinity in Echinochloa crus-galli.
abstract: Herbicide resistance and soil salinization increasingly co-occur in rice paddies, yet how evolved penoxsulam resistance shapes the fitness of barnyardgrass (Echinochloa crus-galli) under combined salt and herbicide stress remains poorly understood. This study aimed to resolve the physiological and molecular basis of such cross-stress tolerance. Using a fully factorial design contrasting a penoxsulam-resistant (AH-225, RI = 4.21) and a susceptible (HN-232) biotype under 100 mm NaCl, 25 g a.i. ha-1 penoxsulam, and their combination, integrated phenotyping, untargeted metabolomics and RNA-seq revealed that the two biotypes were equally suppressed by salinity alone but diverged under penoxsulam exposure; under combined dual stress, resistant plants maintained 3.78-fold greater aboveground biomass, corresponding to an antagonistic buffering interaction quantified by Bliss independence modelling. Sequencing of eight ALS codons associated with target-site resistance detected no mutation in either biotype, indicating a nontarget-site (metabolic) basis of resistance. Metabolome-wide profiling showed that susceptible plants mounted a costly defensive burst of flavonoids and anthocyanins (Group 9), whereas resistant plants preferentially sustained lignin precursors and accumulated rosin-type diterpenoids (Group 15). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis resolved two antagonistic transcriptional programs: a damage-responsive module marked by the DNA-repair gene MSH4, and a growth-homeostasis module enriched in lipid transfer proteins. Penoxsulam resistance in E. crus-galli operates through constitutive homeostasis maintenance and targeted carbon partitioning rather than amplified defence, providing a mechanistic framework for integrated resistance management in saline paddy fields. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: Intratumoral co-activation of ERV transcription and RNA virus-sensing is associated with radiotherapy-induced immune response and abscopal effect.
abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) transforms tumors into in situ vaccines that trigger antitumor immunity. However, the relevant pathways remain largely unelucidated, limiting clinical translation. Herein, we developed a hybrid dry-lab/wet-lab approach integrating systems-level immune phenotypes following homogenous or spatially fractionated RT (SFRT) with transcriptomic profiling of irradiated tumors. By combining feature extraction with machine-learning, including multilayer perceptron modeling, we ranked predictors of immune infiltration and patient survivability for each RT type. RT induced coordinated upregulation of viral RNA-binding proteins (OASes and RIG I-like receptors) along with endogenous retrovirus (ERV) RNAs predominately 400-800 bp long, which may serve as their ligands. During abscopal responses, OASes and ERV transcripts were co-induced and shared between irradiated and distant tumors. SFRT triggered earlier activation of OAS signaling versus homogenous RT. Our findings highlight ERVs as underappreciated contributors to RT-induced antitumor immunity and their interactions with intratumoral cytosolic sensors as potential novel biomarkers in precision radio-oncology.

title: B-Cell Maturation Antigen T-Cell Engager Therapy in a Patient With Refractory Plasma Cell Clonal Cryoglobulinemia Unmasked by RNA-Based Immunoglobulin Sequencing.
abstract: Treatment of type I cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis depends on identifying the monoclonal clone responsible for cryoglobulin secretion. We report the case of a woman in whom the culprit clone proved exceptionally difficult to detect, making treatment guidance highly uncertain. Using the RACE RepSeq technique combined with innovative bone marrow cell sorting, and later through direct visualization within the kidney, we identified a likely plasma cell clone responsible for the cryoglobulin. Despite targeted interventions, the disease remained refractory to conventional therapies, teclistamab, a bispecific T-cell-engaging antibody redirecting T cells against plasma cells, achieved efficacy. Finally, residual disease monitoring was possible through a novel targeted mass spectrometry approach (MALDI-TOF MS), sensitive enough to visualize the cryoglobulin M-protein. This case highlights the challenges of detecting elusive monoclonal clones in many monoclonal gammopathies of renal significance, illustrates the potential of advanced diagnostic tools, and underscores the promise of T-cell-redirecting therapies in refractory cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis.

title: The SRY-box transcription factor 2 (SOX2)-cell division control protein 10 (CDC10) axis regulates bovine myogenesis via the Akt, ERK1/2, and p38 signaling pathway.
abstract: Myogenesis is considered an important biological basis for meat production performance in livestock. The CDC10 gene, which is involved in cellular proliferation, is located within a genomic region associated with quantitative trait loci for growth traits in several cattle breeds. However, its potential regulatory role and underlying molecular mechanisms in bovine muscle development remain unclear. In this study, our results suggested that CDC10 may inhibit the proliferation of bovine skeletal muscle satellite cells while promoting their differentiation. We further found that the transcription factor SOX2 may contribute to the regulation of CDC10 expression through preferential binding to the motif containing the C allele of the g.61710450G > C SNP in the CDC10 promoter. Furthermore, RNA transcriptome sequencing and subsequent analyses suggested that the effects of CDC10 on bovine skeletal muscle satellite cell myogenesis may be associated with changes in the Akt, ERK1/2, and p38 signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings support a potential role for the SOX2-CDC10 regulatory axis in bovine myogenesis, possibly involving the Akt, ERK1/2, and p38 signaling pathways.

title: Cycloastragenol suppresses LPS-induced macrophage inflammation and promotes M2 polarization via TLR4/NF-κB signaling and SIRT1-related regulation.
abstract: Astragalus has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine for tonifying qi and supporting defensive functions. Cycloastragenol (CAG), a characteristic triterpenoid aglycone derived from Astragalus saponins, has emerging pharmacological relevance in immune and inflammatory regulation, but its role in macrophage inflammatory regulation and phenotypic remodeling remains insufficiently defined. To investigate the effects of CAG on lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophage inflammation and phenotypic remodeling, focusing on Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and the involvement of sirtuin 1 (SIRT1). RAW 264.7 macrophages were pretreated with CAG before LPS stimulation. Cytokine secretion, phenotype markers, and inflammatory signaling were evaluated by ELISA, immunofluorescence, reverse transcription quantitative PCR, and Western blotting. SIRT1-targeting small interfering RNA was used for functional evaluation. Network pharmacology prioritized candidate targets, while two acute inflammatory tissue transcriptomes and a normal human immune atlas provided expression context. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations explored candidate CAG-protein interactions. Compared with LPS alone, CAG at 20 μmol/L reduced TNF-α from 56.15 ± 2.17 to 25.80 ± 1.87 pg/mL and IL-1β from 93.55 ± 2.66 to 44.49 ± 2.85 pg/mL (mean ± standard deviation; both Tukey-adjusted P < 0.0001). At this concentration, CAG decreased inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and CD86 and increased arginase-1 (ARG1) and CD206. Network pharmacology prioritized TLR4 and SIRT1. Wounded human skin and LPS-exposed mouse lungs showed increased expression of the gene encoding monocyte chemoattractant protein-1-induced protein 1 (MCPIP1). The human atlas detected transcripts for these regulators in macrophages and monocytes. CAG attenuated TLR4/NF-κB signaling and partially restored SIRT1 expression. During CAG treatment, SIRT1 silencing increased TLR4 expression, the phosphorylated/total p65 ratio, iNOS, and CD86 and decreased ARG1, weakening the signaling and phenotypic effects of CAG. Docking and simulations suggested possible CAG-protein interactions. CAG attenuated LPS-induced macrophage inflammation and favored M2-associated phenotypic remodeling, with SIRT1 contributing to these effects. These findings support CAG as a promising Astragalus-derived immunomodulatory candidate and provide a basis for further exploration of its clinical translational potential.

title: Lack of NRF2 expression alters the dynamics of stress granules promoting the aggregation of ALS disease-associated proteins.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron death. Although ALS pathogenesis is multifactorial, increasing evidence highlights a close interplay between dysfunction of RNA metabolism and redox imbalance in disease progression. Redox perturbation converges with RNA dysregulation at the level of the dynamics of stress granules, transient ribonucleoprotein assemblies implicated in protein aggregation, in ALS. The redox-sensitive transcription factor NRF2 (Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2) plays a pivotal role in cellular homeostasis, yet its function and regulation remain poorly defined in ALS. In this study, we explore how NRF2 modulates stress granule dynamics under oxidative and non-oxidative stress conditions. Using live-cell imaging, we reveal that NRF2 deficiency enhances the formation of stress granules in response to oxidative and non-oxidative stressors, facilitates their persistence, and promotes increased stress granule recruitment of ALS-linked proteins such as TDP-43 and FUS. Likewise, we uncover a protective role of pharmacological NRF2 activation in limiting exacerbated stress granule responses in iPSC-derived motor neurons from C9orf72-ALS patients and show how NRF2 activation can impact TDP-43 aggregation and loss of function in SH-SY5Y cells. Together, these findings position NRF2 as a crucial integrator of redox signalling and RNA metabolism in ALS pathogenesis. Targeting NRF2 may offer novel therapeutic avenues to counteract the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, dysfunctional stress granule dynamics, and protein aggregation in motor neuron disease.

title: Advances in guide RNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated therapeutic RNA editing.
abstract: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) convert adenosine positioned within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to inosine (A-to-I). This reaction can be redirected to a specific target transcript by exogenous guide RNAs (gRNAs) that recruit abundant endogenous ADARs without the need for exogenous protein delivery. Approximately 16,000 pathogenic G > A mutations are correctable by A-to-I conversion, thus representing a broad scope for therapeutic A-to-I editing. This review covers the key advances in gRNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing. We first discuss how ADAR biology informs rational gRNA design. We then survey gRNA design strategies that increase on-target editing efficiency and diminish bystander editing. Delivery modalities are then discussed for both unmodified and modified gRNAs as a strategy to minimize transcriptome-wide off-target editing. We conclude by outlining the outstanding challenges and future opportunities, including computational gRNA design, to guide the next generation of gRNAs towards the path of approved RNA editing medicines.

title: USP14 promotes malignant pleural mesothelioma progression and suppresses autophagy by stabilizing the YAP1-TEAD4 axis.
abstract: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options and poor prognosis. Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) modulate protein turnover and participate in tumor progression, yet the biological function of ubiquitin‑specific protease 14 (USP14) in MPM remains poorly defined. We examined USP14 expression in public datasets and MPM cell lines. Lentiviral‑mediated short hairpin RNA (shRNA) was used to knock down USP14. Functional assays including colony‑formation, Transwell, flow cytometry, xenograft model, autophagic flux detection, co‑immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination and rescue overexpression experiments were performed to explore biological roles and molecular mechanisms of USP14 in MPM. In this study, USP14 was significantly up‑regulated in MPM cell lines. USP14 silencing inhibited cell proliferation, clonogenicity, migration and invasion, promoted apoptosis in vitro, and suppressed xenograft tumor growth. USP14 depletion induced autophagy activation. Mechanistically, USP14 bound to YAP1, removed its poly‑ubiquitin modification and stabilized YAP1 protein to sustain TEAD4 activation. Overexpression of YAP1 or TEAD4 reversed the malignant phenotypes and autophagy triggered by USP14 knockdown. Our findings identify USP14 as one of the major oncogenic DUBs that drives MPM progression through maintenance of YAP1-TEAD4 signaling while inhibiting autophagy. Targeting USP14 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MPM.

title: Antigen-Experience Imprints Integrin Expression in Human B Cells.
abstract: Integrins are critical regulators of lymphocyte adhesion and migration, shaping immune responses by directing cells to specific tissues. In B cells, integrin expression is dynamically regulated during differentiation and activation, yet it is incompletely understood whether immunization and infection influence these pathways. Here, we investigated the expression and regulation of the α4β1 and α4β7 integrins across circulating human B-cell subsets in adults and children following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and/or infection. By combining flow cytometry, bulk and paired single-cell RNA and VDJ sequencing, and antigen-specific analyses, we show that naïve and early memory B cells predominantly express β7, while antigen experience drives the emergence of two integrin-imprinted memory lineages characterized by β7 or β1 expression. The highest integrin levels were observed in activated memory B cells (actMBCs) and plasmablasts, indicating enhanced migratory potential. Integrin expression was linked both to the maturation stage and to the immunoglobulin isotype. Importantly, SARS-CoV-2 infection-either before or after vaccination-significantly increased the frequency of β1-expressing memory B cells in both adults and children, particularly among spike-specific actMBCs. Single-cell analyses further identified distinct actMBC subsets with divergent integrin profiles and activation dynamics. Together, our findings demonstrate that respiratory viral infection imprints durable migratory programs on antigen-specific B cells, favoring α4β1 expression, with implications for tissue targeting and the design of next-generation mucosal vaccines.

title: hsa-miR-155-5p concentration as a determinant of leptinemia in umbilical cord plasma.
abstract: Childhood obesity, which is reaching alarming prevalence worldwide, is associated with long-term adverse metabolic and cardiovascular health outcomes and often persists into adulthood. Investigating the mechanisms responsible for weight gain in early life is essential to better understand and prevent obesity and its related comorbidities. Leptin is a hormone primarily secreted by adipocytes. It suppresses appetite and increases energy expenditure through neonatal programming of the hypothalamic neural circuits responsible for regulation of food intake. The mechanisms regulating leptinemia are not fully understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), short RNA molecules repressing protein synthesis of their target genes and secreted in bloodstream, may play a role. To identify circulating miRNAs whose levels are associated with leptinemia in umbilical cord plasma (UCP), the present study quantified the miRNAs from 273 newborns in the Gen3G prospective birth cohort using next-generation sequencing (NGS). A total of 73 miRNAs were associated with leptinemia (P≤0.05) in UCP. Of these, miR-183-5p and miR-155-5p were selected to be requantified by digital PCR for 201 of these newborns based on the strength of their association [Log2(fold-change)=0.22, P=0.0007 and Log2(fold-change)=-0.14, P=0.005, respectively]. Association with leptinemia was replicated for miR-155-5p (Pearson correlations: NGS, r=-0.13, P=0.03; dPCR, r=-0.12, P=0.04). Biological pathways analysis showed that miR-155-5p is predicted to target the leptin receptor mRNA. These findings suggest miR-155-5p may influence leptinemia in UCP and contribute to early-life adiposity programming.

title: Aloe-Emodin Attenuates Cisplatin-Induced Ferroptotic Osteogenic Impairment in Bone Marrow Stromal Cells Through a YAP1-Dependent Mechanism.
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced bone loss (CIBL) is an important complication of anticancer treatment and is partly attributed to impaired osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow stromal/mesenchymal cells (BMSCs). Aloe-emodin (AE), a natural anthraquinone compound, has shown tissue-protective and anti-ferroptotic activities in chemotherapy-related organ injury. Its role in cisplatin (CDDP)-induced osteogenic impairment remains unclear. To investigate whether ferroptosis contributes to CDDP-induced osteogenic suppression in BMSCs and whether AE protects against this process through a Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1)-dependent mechanism. The anti-tumor effective concentration of CDDP was determined in 143B osteosarcoma cells. ST2 cells and primary mouse and human BMSCs were used to establish an in vitro model of CDDP-induced osteogenic impairment. Ferroptosis-related changes were assessed by Fe2⁺ accumulation, reactive oxygen species (ROS)/lipid peroxidation (LPO), and expression of related markers. Osteogenic differentiation was evaluated by alkaline phosphatase (AP) staining and osteogenic gene expression. RNA-seq, pharmacological inhibition, and Yap1 knockdown were used for mechanistic analysis. CDDP concentrations that inhibited 143B cells also induced ferroptosis in ST2 cells, characterized by Fe2⁺ accumulation, increased ROS and LPO, decreased glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), and impaired osteogenic differentiation. Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) alleviated ferroptotic stress and restored osteogenesis. Under co-treatment conditions, AE reduced Fe2⁺ overload, ROS and LPO, restored anti-ferroptotic defenses, and improved osteogenic differentiation in ST2 cells as well as in primary mouse and human BMSCs. AE did not protect 143B cells from CDDP cytotoxicity, but further enhanced CDDP-mediated growth inhibition. Mechanistically, CDDP suppressed YAP1 expression and nuclear localization, whereas AE restored YAP1 activity. Verteporfin and Yap1 knockdown abolished AE-mediated protection. AE protects BMSCs from CDDP-induced ferroptotic osteogenic impairment through a YAP1-dependent mechanism without compromising the anti-osteosarcoma effect of CDDP in vitro.

title: Simiao Pill ameliorates collagen-induced arthritis in association with gut-joint axis modulation and attenuation of cGAS-STING signaling.
abstract: Simiao Pill formula (SM), composed of Phellodendron chinense C.K.Schneid., Atractylodes lancea (Thunb.) DC., Achyranthes bidentata Blume, and Coix lacryma-jobi var. ma-yuen (Rom.Caill.) Stapf, is a traditional Chinese herbal formula historically used for damp-heat Bi syndrome and commonly applied to the management of rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-related arthralgia symptoms. However, its anti-arthritic mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This study evaluated the anti-arthritic effects of SM in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) and examined whether these effects were associated with gut-joint axis-related alterations and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling. A CIA mouse model was established and treated with SM for 6 weeks. Arthritis severity, joint pathology, bone erosion, serum cytokines, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, colonic histology, and tight junction proteins were assessed. Gut microbiota and colonic content metabolites were analyzed using 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. cGAS-STING pathway proteins were examined in joint and colonic tissues. A separate antibiotic-induced microbiota perturbation cohort was used to assess the contribution of gut microbiota to high-dose SM (SM-H) efficacy. SM reduced arthritis scores and spleen index in CIA mice. It decreased serum IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ levels, increased IL-10 production, and alleviated synovitis, cartilage damage, and bone erosion. SM also improved colonic histological abnormalities, enhanced colonic ZO-1 and Occludin expression, and reduced serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein levels, suggesting improvement of intestinal barrier-related indicators. Gut microbiota and metabolomics analyses showed that SM-H reshaped gut microbial composition and colonic content metabolic profiles, particularly involving aromatic amino acid and vitamin-related metabolism. Correlation analysis linked representative microbial taxa and metabolites with arthritis severity, inflammatory responses, intestinal barrier markers, and bone parameters. Moreover, SM suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation in both joint and colonic tissues. Under antibiotic exposure, the anti-arthritic, barrier-related, and cGAS-STING-inhibitory responses associated with SM-H were attenuated. SM ameliorated CIA in association with coordinated changes in gut microbial composition, colonic content metabolism, intestinal barrier-related indicators, systemic inflammation, and cGAS-STING signaling. Antibiotic exposure attenuated multiple SM-H-associated responses, supporting a contribution of microbiota-associated processes to the therapeutic response, although microbiota-specific causality was not established.

title: Tenascin‑C promotes pulmonary fibrosis via responding to oxidative stress and amplifying profibrotic signaling.
abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive and often fatal lung disease, and effective therapies remain limited, largely because its underlying pathogenic mechanisms are not fully understood. Here, we investigated the stage-specific role of the extracellular matrix protein Tenascin-C (TNC) in pulmonary fibrogenesis. Analysis of four independent human transcriptomic datasets identified 195 differentially expressed genes shared across datasets, among which TNC was markedly upregulated and functionally enriched in fibrosis- and matrix-associated pathways. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis indicated that TNC expression was primarily detected in fibroblasts and was associated with fibrotic differentiation. Experiments in mice with bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis further confirmed progressive TNC upregulation and demonstrated its colocalization with α-SMA+ myofibroblasts. Functionally, TNC deficiency inhibited fibroblast proliferation, migration, and activation in vitro and significantly improved survival and attenuated collagen deposition and fibrotic damage in vivo. Notably, TNC exhibited a temporal functional switch during disease progression. During the early inflammatory phase, TNC responded to oxidative stress and promoted the recruitment of CD68+ macrophages, thereby accelerating inflammatory infiltration. This effect was further confirmed in fibroblast-macrophage co-cultures treated with H2O2. During the late fibrotic phase, TNC amplified the fibrotic cascade by enhancing TGF-β-driven fibroblast activation and increasing α-SMA and collagen I expression. Overall, our findings establish TNC as a key spatiotemporal hub linking the oxidative stress-inflammation-fibrosis cascade, making it a promising therapeutic target for pulmonary fibrosis.

title: Sodium Butyrate Ameliorates Hepatic Steatosis and Insulin Resistance in MASLD Models With Concurrent Alterations in AMPK and PI3K/AKT Signaling.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is characterized by dysregulated glucose and lipid metabolism and is closely linked to insulin resistance (IR). Sodium butyrate (NaB) is a short-chain fatty acid with reported metabolic benefits, but its effects on MASLD-related IR remain unclear. This study investigated the therapeutic efficacy of NaB in both palmitate (PA)-induced insulin-resistant hepatocytes and high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MASLD in mice and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms responsible for its effects. We evaluated the effects of NaB in PA-treated HepG2 cells and in C57BL/6 mice fed an HFD for 16 weeks followed by 8 weeks of oral NaB administration.
